questions.question: In what year was the Battle of Hastings, at which William of Normandy defeated King Harold, fought?
questions.note: Fought on 14 October 1066, it ended with Harold's death and William being crowned King of England in Westminster Abbey that Christmas Day.

questions.question: From which animal's milk is Roquefort cheese traditionally made?
questions.note: Roquefort was granted France's very first AOC in 1925 and is ripened in the natural Combalou caves at Roquefort-sur-Soulzon.

questions.question: What is the name of the strait at the narrowest point of the English Channel, between England and France?
questions.note: The crossing here is just about 33 km (21 miles) wide, from the South Foreland near Dover to Cap Gris-Nez near Calais.

questions.question: In which Warwickshire market town was William Shakespeare born in 1564?
questions.note: His half-timbered birthplace on Henley Street still stands and is open to visitors today.

questions.question: In what year was the first Tour de France held?
questions.note: The race was dreamed up by the newspaper L'Auto to boost its sales, and the first winner was Maurice Garin.

questions.question: The fabric name "denim" comes from "serge de ___", after a city in southern France. Which city?
questions.note: The sturdy twill was 'serge de Nîmes'; the silent final 's' helped it slur into plain 'denim' in English by the mid-1800s.

questions.question: In which Normandy city was Joan of Arc burned at the stake in 1431?
questions.note: She was burned in the Place du Vieux-Marché on 30 May 1431 and her ashes thrown into the Seine; she was declared a saint nearly five centuries later.

questions.question: Under its protected status, which is the only meat allowed in a traditional Cornish pasty?
questions.note: Since gaining protected status in 2011, a genuine Cornish pasty may contain only beef, potato, swede and onion, and must be crimped on the side, never the top.

questions.question: What is the longest river in France?
questions.note: The Loire runs about 1,020 km and is famed both for its string of Renaissance chateaux and for being called the last wild river in Europe.

questions.question: Which Charles Dickens novel, set in London and Paris during the French Revolution, opens with the line 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'?
questions.note: It ends with the lawyer Sydney Carton going to the guillotine in another man's place, declaring 'it is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done.'

questions.question: In what year was the first Wimbledon Championship held?
questions.note: The very first tournament was staged partly to pay for repairs to the club's broken pony-drawn lawn roller.

questions.question: In which year did euro banknotes and coins first enter circulation, replacing the franc as everyday cash in France?
questions.note: The euro existed as an 'invisible' accounting currency from 1999, but the physical cash changeover on 1 January 2002 was the biggest in history.

questions.question: The Entente Cordiale, the set of agreements that ended centuries of on-off hostility between Britain and France, was signed in which year?
questions.note: Signed on 8 April 1904 by Lord Lansdowne and ambassador Paul Cambon, it paved the way for the two nations to fight side by side in the First World War.

questions.question: Gamay is the principal red grape variety of which French wine region?
questions.note: Duke Philip the Bold banned Gamay from Burgundy in the 1300s for being inferior to Pinot Noir, which pushed it south to Beaujolais.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom?
questions.note: At 1,345 m near Fort William, 'the Ben' once had a Victorian weather observatory manned year-round on its summit.

questions.question: Claude Monet's 1872 painting of a hazy harbour at dawn, whose title inspired the name of a whole art movement, is called what?
questions.note: The harbour is Le Havre, Monet's hometown, and critic Louis Leroy seized on the title to mock the group as 'Impressionists' — the insult stuck as the movement's name.

questions.question: Which country joined rugby's Five Nations in 2000 to create the Six Nations Championship?
questions.note: Italy marked their arrival by beating Scotland 34-20 in their very first Six Nations match.

questions.question: The spoken distress call "mayday" is a phonetic spelling of which French phrase meaning "help me"?
questions.note: A radio officer at Croydon Airport coined it in 1923 so pilots crossing the Channel to Le Bourget could be understood by both sides.

questions.question: Which English king led his heavily outnumbered army to victory over the French at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
questions.note: English longbowmen cut down the French knights floundering in the mud; Shakespeare later immortalised the king's 'band of brothers' speech.

questions.question: The French kitchen phrase 'mise en place' translates literally as what?
questions.note: The great French chef Auguste Escoffier is often credited with formalising the practice in professional kitchens.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain in the Alps and in western Europe?
questions.note: At 4,808 m it straddles the France-Italy border, its summit a permanent dome of snow and ice.

questions.question: Which British painter created The Fighting Temeraire, showing an old warship towed away to be scrapped, exhibited in 1839?
questions.note: The veteran ship had fought at Trafalgar in 1805, and Turner sets her last journey against a blazing sunset as the age of sail gives way to steam.

questions.question: In which French coastal town was the game of pétanque invented around 1910?
questions.note: It was devised so a rheumatic player could throw with 'pieds tanqués' — feet planted — instead of taking the traditional run-up.

questions.question: What is the French custom of greeting someone with a light kiss on each cheek called?
questions.note: The number varies wildly by region — usually two, but three in parts of the south and even four in some départements.

questions.question: What was the code name for the overall Allied invasion of Normandy that began on D-Day, 6 June 1944?
questions.note: Troops landed across five beaches code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, with the seaborne assault phase itself code-named Neptune.

questions.question: The village of Cheddar, which gave its name to the cheese, lies in which English county?
questions.note: Cheesemakers once aged their cheddar in the cool, damp caves of Cheddar Gorge, which acted as natural refrigerators.

questions.question: Which is the largest of the Channel Islands?
questions.note: Lying only about 14 miles off the Normandy coast, Jersey is the biggest Channel Island at roughly 45 square miles.

questions.question: Under what real name was the playwright Molière born?
questions.note: He adopted the stage name Molière as a young actor and, fittingly for a man of the theatre, was taken fatally ill on stage while performing in his own play The Imaginary Invalid.

questions.question: In cricket, the Ashes is a Test series contested between England and which other country?
questions.note: The name comes from an 1882 mock obituary in the Sporting Times mourning English cricket, whose 'body will be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia'.

questions.question: A dead-end residential street is often called a "cul-de-sac" — French that literally means the bottom of a ___?
questions.note: Estate agents love the term, but in French 'cul' is a decidedly cheeky word for 'bottom'.
